short_description: Log4Shell: unauthenticated remote code execution in Apache Log4j2 via attacker-controlled JNDI lookups.
Shellshock: crafted environment variables let an attacker run arbitrary commands via GNU Bash.
Apache Struts2 remote code execution via a malicious Content-Type header; the vector used in the 2017 Equifax breach.
Zerologon: a cryptographic flaw in the Netlogon protocol lets an attacker instantly take over a Windows domain controller.
BlueKeep: wormable, unauthenticated remote code execution in Windows Remote Desktop Services.
Spring4Shell: a data-binding flaw in Spring MVC/WebFlux on JDK 9+ enables remote code execution.
ProxyShell: a pre-authentication remote code execution chain against Microsoft Exchange Server.
SQL injection in Progress MOVEit Transfer, mass-exploited by the Cl0p ransomware group to steal data.
Drupalgeddon2: remote code execution in Drupal core from insufficient input sanitization.
ProxyLogon: a server-side request forgery in Microsoft Exchange Server enabling pre-auth remote code execution.
A Kubernetes API server request-proxying flaw lets an authenticated user escalate to arbitrary backend access, risking full cluster compromise.
A flaw in TLS/SSL session renegotiation lets a man-in-the-middle inject data into an otherwise secure connection.
EternalBlue: an SMBv1 remote code execution flaw in Windows, the exploit behind the 2017 WannaCry and NotPetya outbreaks.
PrintNightmare: remote code execution and privilege escalation in the Windows Print Spooler service.
Heartbleed: an OpenSSL heartbeat-extension bug leaks sensitive process memory (keys, passwords, session data) to remote attackers.
'Baron Samedit': a heap-based buffer overflow in sudo lets any local user escalate to root.
PwnKit: a memory-corruption bug in Polkit's pkexec allows local privilege escalation to root on most Linux distributions.
Dirty COW: a race condition in the Linux kernel's memory management allows local privilege escalation.
CurveBall: a Windows CryptoAPI flaw lets an attacker forge certificate signatures and spoof trusted software or TLS endpoints.
Follina: remote code execution via the Windows Support Diagnostic Tool (MSDT), triggered from a malicious Office document.
A heap buffer overflow in the libwebp image library, exploited in the wild via malicious WebP images in browsers and apps.
Dirty Pipe: a Linux kernel flaw lets unprivileged users overwrite data in supposedly read-only files.
A runc container-runtime flaw lets a malicious container overwrite the host runc binary and gain code execution on the host.
A 17-year-old memory-corruption bug in Microsoft Office's Equation Editor enables remote code execution via a crafted document.
A Kubernetes kube-proxy flaw lets neighboring hosts or pods reach services that were meant to be bound only to localhost.
A WinRAR flaw executes attacker code when a victim opens a specially crafted archive, even though the file preview looks benign.
Spectre (variant 1): a CPU speculative-execution side channel lets code read memory it shouldn't have access to.
Spectre (variant 2, branch target injection): a speculative-execution side channel affecting most modern CPUs.
Meltdown: a CPU flaw lets an unprivileged process read protected kernel memory via out-of-order execution.
A NULL pointer dereference in OpenSSL's X509_issuer_and_serial_hash() can crash an application processing a malicious certificate.
An OpenSSL TLS 1.2 renegotiation bug lets a malicious client crash a server by sending a crafted ClientHello.
OpenSSH's client-side 'roaming' feature could leak private key material to a malicious or compromised server.
A buffer overflow in sudo's get_process_ttyname() allows privilege escalation on Linux systems with SELinux enabled.
A Kubernetes admission-controller validation bypass lets a node-update request alter a pod's specification after admission checks.
A Windows LSA spoofing flaw, related to the PetitPotam technique, can be abused to force NTLM authentication and relay it to a domain controller.
A Microsoft Exchange Server security-feature bypass, one of the vulnerabilities chained together in the ProxyShell attack.
An OpenSSH authentication timing discrepancy lets a remote attacker enumerate valid usernames on a target system.
BEAST: a chosen-plaintext attack against TLS 1.0/SSL 3.0 block-cipher (CBC) suites that can recover encrypted session data.
DROWN: a cross-protocol attack that abuses legacy SSLv2 support on a server to break the encryption of modern TLS sessions.
FREAK: a flaw that lets an attacker force a TLS connection to downgrade to weak, export-grade RSA encryption.
POODLE: a padding-oracle flaw in SSL 3.0 that lets an attacker decrypt data by forcing a protocol downgrade.
Logjam: a weakness in Diffie-Hellman key exchange that can be abused to force a downgrade to export-grade (512-bit) cryptography.
Lucky Thirteen: a timing side channel in TLS/DTLS CBC-mode padding that can leak plaintext from encrypted sessions.
CRIME: a compression side-channel attack against TLS/SSL that can recover secret session data such as cookies.
SSH sessions using CBC-mode ciphers are vulnerable to partial plaintext recovery by a network attacker.
Raccoon Attack: a timing flaw in the TLS specification's Diffie-Hellman handling that can leak session data if a DH secret is reused across connections.
OpenSSL did not properly validate Diffie-Hellman parameters, making it easier to recover a peer's private DH key through repeated handshakes.
A logic error in OpenSSL's legacy SSLv2 rollback-attack check inverted the accept/reject condition in rare legacy configurations.
WordPress core: misuse of the 'set-screen-option' filter's return value could let a low-privileged user save arbitrary user-meta fields.
In certain OpenSSH public-key-plus-agent-forwarding setups, a malicious server could create ambiguity about which server the user's FIDO authentication was actually confirming.
